findings.title: Pin and verify the install script instead of piping curl into sh
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` runs whatever the remote host (or any redirect target, since -L follows redirects) serves at build time, as root in the image. There is no version pin and no checksum or signature check, so a compromised or changed script ends up in every image built from this file, and builds can't be reproduced. The build also hides failures: without `-f`, curl treats an HTTP 404 or 500 as success and passes the error page body to sh. And because Alpine's `/bin/sh -c` has no pipefail, the RUN step's exit status comes from `sh`, not `curl`. A failed or partial download can still produce a 'successful' layer with the install missing or half done.

findings.title: Do not pipe an unverified remote script into sh during build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` runs as root at build time (no USER directive comes before it). It fetches whatever the remote host serves at that moment: there is no version pin, checksum or signature check, and redirects are followed (-L). If that host or any redirect target is compromised, or the script just changes, arbitrary code ends up in the image without anyone noticing, and builds stop being reproducible. curl runs without -f and the shell has no pipefail. So if the server returns an HTTP error, curl still exits 0 and pipes the error page into sh. If the download fails at the network level, sh runs on empty input, the step succeeds and the install is silently skipped (failure goes unnoticed).

findings.title: Do not pipe an unverified remote install script into sh at build time
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` downloads a mutable script and runs it as root in the image build. There is no pinned version, no checksum or signature check, and nothing records what ran. Whoever controls example.com, or anything that redirects it (-L follows redirects), can put arbitrary code into the built image, and two builds of the same commit can produce different images. The build also does not fail on network errors: without `-f`, curl writes an HTTP 404/500 error body into the pipe, and the RUN step's exit status is the exit status of `sh`. Alpine's /bin/sh runs without pipefail, so an error page or a truncated download is either run as shell or quietly does nothing, and the layer is cached as if it succeeded. That is a swallowed failure (TRIGGER D).

findings.title: Stop LoadOrDefault from hiding ErrMissing behind an empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent (src/store.go:9-10). LoadOrDefault drops that error with `v, _ :=` and returns "". A key that is present with the value "" also returns "". Callers of this exported API cannot tell "missing" from "empty value", so they may store, report or act on the fallback as if it were real data. The name also says 'OrDefault', but the caller cannot supply a default. The only possible default is the zero value, and it looks the same as a real empty entry. Nothing in the repo calls this yet, but the public contract itself forces every future caller to mix up failure and a real value.

findings.title: Stop discarding ErrMissing in exported LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: `Load` (src/store.go:7-13) has two outcomes: ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent, and (v, nil) when it is present. A present key can hold "". `LoadOrDefault` drops the error with `v, _ :=` and returns only the string. So a missing key and a key stored as "" both come back as "". Because the function is exported, every caller must treat a missing key as a real empty value and may save or act on it. The name also says "OrDefault", but there is no default parameter. The function always falls back to Go's zero value, "", which is indistinguishable from real data.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Run returned only after every `results <- j*2` had finished. Callers could therefore safely `close(results)` or start draining once Run returned. Now Run returns right after starting len(jobs) goroutines. (1) A caller that closes results after Run returns, which the old version allowed, races the pending sends and panics with 'send on closed channel'. (2) A caller that reads exactly len(jobs) values gets them in random order, so results no longer line up with jobs. (3) ctx is still ignored and the goroutines are detached. If the consumer stops reading (cancellation or early return), every pending goroutine blocks forever on the send. That is one leaked goroutine per job, and nothing can cancel them.

findings.title: Wait for result goroutines before Run returns; honor ctx on send
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Run sent every j*2 itself before returning. When Run returned, all len(jobs) results had been delivered, so a caller could safely do `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` or stop reading. Now lines 7-9 start one goroutine per job and Run returns as soon as they are started. (1) If a caller closes `results` after Run returns, any send that has not happened yet panics with 'send on closed channel'. (2) If the reader stops early or the channel is unbuffered and nobody reads, every pending goroutine blocks forever on `results <-`, which leaks one goroutine per job. ctx cannot cancel them because the sends never check it. (3) Results now arrive in no fixed order, and there is no limit on how many goroutines start (len(jobs)).

findings.title: Wait for spawned sends before Run returns; honor ctx
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Run returned only after every result had been sent to `results`. When Run returned, all work was done, so a caller could `close(results)` or stop reading. Now Run starts one goroutine per job and returns right away, with no WaitGroup or other way to tell when the sends finish. (1) A caller that does the usual `Run(...); close(results)` will hit `panic: send on closed channel` when a goroutine sends late. (2) A caller that reads exactly len(jobs) values and stops, or whose consumer quits early, leaves goroutines blocked on the send forever. `ctx` is never checked, so cancelling it cannot release them. (3) Results now arrive in goroutine scheduling order instead of job order. Run is exported, so this new completion contract is itself the defect, even though nothing in the repo calls Run yet.

findings.title: Restore && so delete requires admin AND same tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, deleting required both session.isAdmin and session.tenantId === record.tenantId. With ||, either condition alone is enough. (1) Admin of tenant A, record in tenant B: isAdmin=true, so the function returns true. That is a cross-tenant delete, which breaks tenant isolation. (2) Non-admin in tenant A, record in tenant A: the tenants match, so it returns true. Any regular user can now delete every record in their tenant, which is a privilege escalation. Both are data-loss paths through an exported authorization predicate.

findings.title: Restore && so delete requires admin AND same tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, delete was allowed only when `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId`. With `||` there are two new ways in. (1) `{isAdmin:true, tenantId:'A'}` with `record.tenantId:'B'` now gets true, so an admin in tenant A can delete tenant B's records. (2) `{isAdmin:false, tenantId:'A'}` with `record.tenantId:'A'` now gets true, so any regular user can delete any record in their tenant, including ones they don't own (`ownerId` is never checked). `canDeleteRecord` is an exported authorization function, so every caller that relies on it now accepts both cases.

findings.title: Restore && so delete needs both admin role and same tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, delete required session.isAdmin AND session.tenantId === record.tenantId. With ||, two cases flip from false to true. (1) Cross-tenant: {isAdmin:true, tenantId:'A'} with record {tenantId:'B'} now returns true, so an admin in one tenant can delete another tenant's records. (2) Missing role: {isAdmin:false, tenantId:'A'} with record {tenantId:'A'} now returns true, so any ordinary user can delete any record in their tenant, including ones they don't own (ownerId is never checked). Both are authorization bypasses on a destructive action and can cause data loss.

findings.title: Don't swallow parse/validation errors: updateFontSize saves defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, parseSettings threw on invalid JSON or wrong field types, so updateFontSize (line 20) stopped before calling save. Now the catch-all at lines 14-16 returns { ...DEFAULTS }, and the caller can't tell a failure apart from settings that really are the defaults. updateFontSize then sets fontSize and calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)) at line 22. Example: raw = '{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"16"}' (fontSize stored as a string) fails the check at line 12. The function returns theme 'light', and save writes '{"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}'. The user's 'dark' theme is permanently overwritten. Invalid JSON is also replaced with defaults without any error. Because parseSettings is exported, every caller now has to treat a parse failure as if it were real data.

findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, bad JSON or a wrong field type made parseSettings throw. That error escaped updateFontSize before save() ran, so stored data stayed untouched. findings.title: Restore the defensive copy so apply_values stops changing the caller's df
findings.whyItBreaks: At base, `apply_values` worked on `result = df.copy()` and returned that copy, so the caller's DataFrame was never touched. At head, `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` writes straight into the caller's object and returns that same object. Any caller that keeps the original frame (to compare, reuse, retry, or apply several mappings to one source) now has its data overwritten without warning. findings.title: Restore df.copy() so apply_values no longer changes the caller's DataFrame

Now `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` writes straight into the caller's object and hands back the same object. A caller that keeps using the original df after the call will silently see the new values, for example when comparing before and after, reusing one source frame with different mappings, or holding a cached or shared frame. In that case Save returns nil for a file that may be truncated or not persisted. Save is exported and returns error, so any caller is forced to treat a failed save as a success and may go on to rely on data that was never written.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the only authentication gate for webhooks: handle() returns 401 unless it passes (app/webhook.py:14-15). Python's `str ==` stops at the first character that differs, so how long the check takes depends on how much of the attacker's signature matches. An attacker who can send repeated requests can use that timing to recover the expected hex HMAC for a chosen payload, then get the payload past verification and into processor(payload). The old code used hmac.compare_digest, which takes the same time regardless of where the strings differ, to prevent exactly this.

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison for webhook HMAC signature

An attacker can time repeated requests to `handle` (app/webhook.py:14), work out the valid signature one hex character at a time for any payload they choose, and get past the 401 gate so `processor(payload)` runs on forged input. The removed `hmac.compare_digest` call is the standard defence against exactly this attack.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify()

The old code used `hmac.compare_digest`, whose timing does not depend on where the inputs differ. findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside one `with db.transaction():` block, so they all committed or all rolled back together. (1) If either UPDATE fails (bad to_acct, constraint, connection drop), the committed ledger row stays but no balances change, so the ledger and the accounts disagree. The reviewer then reports findings on code the PR never touched, and inlineComments (line 63) lets those findings through as inline comments on paths that are not in the PR. If PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checked-out HEAD (for example a pull_request checkout of the merge ref), the reviewed patch no longer matches the commit_id the review is posted against (lines 85, 124).

findings.title: Restore merge-base so the review diff only contains the PR's own commits
findings.whyItBreaks: On line 138, baseSha comes from PR_BASE_SHA when it is set. In GitHub that is normally pull_request.base.sha, which is the tip of the base branch, not where the PR forked. The removed `git merge-base baseSha headSha` step used to turn that tip into the fork point. Now `git diff baseSha HEAD` is a straight two-point diff. So every commit that landed on main after the PR branched appears reversed in `patch`, and its files go into `changedFiles`/`changedPaths` via changedFileSet (line 57, same two-point diff). The reviewer then sees changes the PR never made, can file findings on them and classify their surfaces, and may request changes on unrelated code. inlineComments (line 63) then lets comments through on paths that are not in the PR. GitHub rejects those with a 422, and the catch at line 96 falls back to a body-only review, so every inline comment is lost.

findings.title: Diff against headSha, not the checked-out HEAD
findings.whyItBreaks: headSha can come from PR_HEAD_SHA (line 137). It is what goes into the bundle (line 165), and the review is posted against it (commit_id, line 85) with side RIGHT line numbers. The old code diffed against headSha. The new code diffs against the working tree's HEAD (line 139, and line 57 for file names). When those two differ, the patch and the reviewer's line numbers describe a different tree from the commit the comments are attached to. One example is actions/checkout's default refs/pull/N/merge commit on pull_request events. When that happens, inline comments land on the wrong lines or fail, and the bundle's headSha does not match its patch.

findings.title: Restore function replacers so `$` patterns in diff/bundle aren't expanded
findings.whyItBreaks: When `String.prototype.replace` gets a string as its second argument, it treats `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'` and `$$` as special patterns. The bundle JSON (lines 23-26) and `bundle.patch` (line 33) contain untrusted diff text, and the candidate findings (line 32) contain model output. Shell scripts, JS template literals, regexes and Makefiles routinely include text like `$$`, `$&` or `$'`. With this change, `$'` pulls in the rest of the template after the placeholder, `` $` `` pulls in everything before it, `$&` re-inserts `{{PATCH}}`/`{{BUNDLE}}`, and `$$` collapses to `$`. As a result, the model reviews a diff and code that differ from what was actually submitted. Findings can get the wrong lines or be missed, and prompt instructions can be duplicated into the data section. The `() => ...` replacers that this diff removed avoided all of this, because a function's return value is inserted literally.

findings.title: Restore function replacers so `$` patterns in the bundle or patch stay literal
findings.whyItBreaks: When String.prototype.replace gets a string as its second argument, it treats `$&`, `$'`, `` $` `` and `$$` as special patterns. A function replacer's return value is inserted as-is. The old code used `() => ...` on purpose so that the text it inserts is never pattern-expanded. Now `bundle.patch`, the JSON bundle (which also contains the patch, agentsMd and prMeta) and the candidate findings JSON are all inserted as pattern strings. Real diffs often contain these sequences: shell `$$` (PID), bash `$'...'` ANSI-C quoting, and regex or template code with `$&`. For example, a patch line with `echo $$` becomes `echo $`. A line with `$'\n'` gets the rest of the prompt template after `{{PATCH}}` spliced into it, and `$&` becomes the literal `{{PATCH}}`. So the reviewer and critic models get a mangled diff or bundle. That can cause false findings or missed bugs, and can break the critic's JSON output, all without any error.

findings.title: Use function replacers so `$` patterns in diff/bundle are not expanded
findings.whyItBreaks: When the second argument to String.prototype.replace is a string, JavaScript treats `$&`, `$$`, `` $` ``, `$'` and `$<name>` as special patterns. The old code passed `() => ...` so the text went in unchanged. Now the bundle JSON, the candidate findings and `bundle.patch` are inserted as replacement strings. A patch that touches shell or regex code is likely to contain these patterns, e.g. `echo $$`, `$'\n'`, or `"$&"`. `$$` becomes `$`. `$&` becomes the literal `{{PATCH}}`/`{{BUNDLE}}`. `` $` `` and `$'` paste in the whole prompt template before or after the placeholder. The model then reviews a diff that differs from the real change, and the bundle JSON can come out malformed or with the prompt pasted in. Nothing reports an error, so reviews can quietly miss or invent findings. Model-produced findings text can also contain `$`, so the critic prompt is affected too.

findings.title: Restore commit_id in fallback review POST to pin the reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: postReview is given the exact headSha that was diffed and reviewed (runGithub @src/adapters/github.ts:141-144, call @183). The main path pins the review to that commit with `commit_id: headSha` (@89). The fallback runs whenever the main path throws, and it no longer sends commit_id. GitHub's create-review endpoint then defaults to the PR's latest commit. A review can take minutes. If someone pushes in that window, a REQUEST_CHANGES or COMMENT verdict and its body get attached to a newer commit that was never reviewed. The PR then shows the verdict as covering code it never looked at, so changes requested on old code show up against new code, and a pass shows up against unreviewed code. The check run is still pinned to headSha (@128), so the review and the check now point at different commits. Before this change both paths pinned the same SHA.

findings.title: Restore commit_id in fallback review POST so it stays pinned to headSha
findings.whyItBreaks: When the first POST (with commit_id=headSha and inline comments, lines 88-99) fails, the fallback posts the review without `commit_id`. GitHub's Create Review API then uses the PR's most recent commit. The fallback is most likely to run when the first POST is rejected, which happens when inline comment lines don't resolve or when headSha is stale after a push or force-push mid-review. In those cases the review body describes findings for headSha, but it gets attached to a newer commit that was never reviewed. GitHub then shows it as current instead of outdated. A REQUEST_CHANGES or COMMENT verdict ends up tied to code Needlefish never saw. It also disagrees with the check run, which still uses head_sha=headSha (line 128). Before this change, the fallback stayed pinned to the reviewed SHA.

findings.title: Restore commit_id in fallback review POST
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary path sends `commit_id: headSha` (line 89), so the review is tied to the exact SHA that was diffed (line 144). The fallback at lines 101-112 runs whenever the primary call throws for any reason. It now sends only `event` and `body`. When commit_id is left out, GitHub's create-review API uses the PR's latest commit at the moment of the POST. The LLM review takes a while, and new commits can be pushed during it. In that case the REQUEST_CHANGES/COMMENT review and its findings get attached to a newer commit that was never reviewed, and they can look current on that code. The check-run posted right after is still pinned to the old `head_sha: headSha` (line 128), so the two outputs now name different commits. Before this change, the fallback pinned the review to the right commit, the same as the primary path.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of coercing them to P1/bug defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, an invalid severity or category, an empty file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, or a non-positive or non-finite lineStart/lineEnd threw a 'malformed finding' error. Now every one of those failures becomes a plausible-looking value. severity 'high' or 'critical' becomes 'P1', so a P0 can be quietly downgraded and junk gets promoted to a merge-blocking P1. An unknown category becomes 'bug'. file becomes '', title becomes 'Untitled finding', lineStart becomes 0, and Number('abc') gives NaN, which passes straight through. Callers cannot tell a fabricated default from a real finding. They will report or gate on findings that point at no file and line 0. This is an exported function, so the contract itself now forces every caller to mix up 'model output was malformed' with 'real P1 bug finding' (TRIGGER D).

findings.title: Restore normalizeReview strict/lenient handling of malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview(raw, false) used to drop malformed findings, and strict mode used to reject the whole review. The `strict` parameter is now gone. JS callers that pass `false` are silently ignored, and the coerced garbage findings are kept in both modes. normalizeFinding also lost its object guard, so a null or non-object entry in `findings` now fails on `raw.severity` with an uninformative TypeError. Lenient mode used to filter that entry out, and strict mode used to give a 'malformed finding: not an object' error.

findings.title: Restore validation instead of defaulting malformed findings to P1/bug
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, an invalid severity or category, an empty file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, or a non-finite or non-positive lineStart/lineEnd made normalizeFinding throw, and normalizeReview passed that error up (strict mode) or dropped the finding (lenient mode). Now each of those signals is replaced with a default. For example, {severity:"critical"} or {severity:"low"} becomes a P1. A missing category becomes "bug". A missing file becomes "". A missing lineStart becomes 0, and lineStart "abc" becomes NaN with no check. Empty whyItBreaks/suggestedFix are accepted. normalizeReview (line 131) returns these as real Finding objects, so anything downstream (verdict, rendering, inline comments) gets a made-up P1 with no file or line, and it looks exactly like a real P1. A typo'd low-severity finding or a garbage object can now block a merge as a P1, and malformed model output no longer triggers the error/retry path. Also, null/primitive input now fails with a generic TypeError (or, for primitives, returns all defaults) instead of the old 'malformed finding' error.

findings.title: Keep normalizeReview's `strict` lenient-drop mode
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview is exported. Its signature used to be (raw, strict = true), and strict=false meant 'drop malformed findings, keep the valid ones'. This diff removes the parameter. TypeScript callers that pass `false` now fail to compile, and JS callers have the argument silently ignored. Because normalizeFinding no longer throws, those callers also stop dropping malformed findings: they get defaulted P1 entries instead. Strict callers stop getting the error that rejected malformed output. Neither old behavior can be selected anymore.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of filling in fake defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, a finding with a bad severity or category, a missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, or a lineStart/lineEnd that was missing or not positive threw a `malformed finding: ...` error. Now each failure becomes a value that looks valid. A bad or missing severity becomes "P1", a blocking severity the model never chose. A missing file becomes "". A missing lineStart becomes 0. Non-numeric line values pass through as NaN: Number("abc") is NaN, and nothing checks the result. Missing text fields become "" or "Untitled finding". The category check also lost its `.trim()`, so "security " with a trailing space, which used to be accepted as security, now silently becomes "bug". normalizeFinding is exported. Anything that reads its result can no longer tell a parse failure from a real finding, so made-up P1 findings with no location reach the review result as if they were real.

findings.title: Restore lenient mode and the null guard in normalizeReview
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizeReview(raw, strict) used to support strict=false, which skipped malformed findings using try/catch. That parameter is gone: callers that pass `false` are now ignored, and malformed findings are kept with fake defaults instead of being dropped. Because normalizeFinding no longer checks for non-objects, a `null` or other non-object entry in `findings` (reached through `raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding)` at line 131) now fails with a TypeError on `raw.severity` instead of the clear `malformed finding: not an object` error. In lenient mode it used to be dropped.

findings.title: Restore -R repo on gh pr view; step runs before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step runs before the actions/checkout step (lines 42-46). With no -R flag and no GH_REPO set, gh gets the repo from the current directory's git remotes. On a fresh or cleaned self-hosted workspace that directory is not a git repo, so `gh pr view` fails. If the workspace still holds an old checkout, gh uses whatever repo is there. The failing `$(...)` sits inside `echo`, so the step does not fail: it writes `head=` and `base=` with empty values. actions/checkout with an empty `ref` falls back to the dispatch ref (for example main), and the review step gets empty PR_HEAD_SHA/PR_BASE_SHA. The result is that every manual workflow_dispatch review either reviews the wrong commit or breaks downstream. Before this change, `-R "$REPO"` (github.repository) made the lookup work with no local repo.

findings.title: Restore -R "$REPO" on gh pr view; it runs before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step (lines 26-40) runs before 'Checkout PR head' (lines 42-46), and nothing in the job sets GH_REPO. With `-R` gone, `gh pr view` has to work out the repository from the current directory's git remote. On a fresh or cleaned runner workspace there is no git repo yet, so gh fails ('not a git repository'). On a reused self-hosted workspace it reads whatever stale checkout is left there. Either way it shouldn't depend on that. The failure is also silent: the command runs inside `echo "head=$(...)"`, and echo exits 0 even when the substituted command fails, so the step passes with `head=` and `base=` empty. Then `actions/checkout` gets `ref: ''` and checks out the default branch (the workflow_dispatch sha), not the PR head. The review step then runs the default branch's src/cli.ts with empty PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA, so a manual review can review the wrong code or fail later with a confusing error. The pull_request path (EVENT_HEAD set) is not affected.

findings.title: Restore -R "$REPO" on gh pr view; this step runs before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step (lines 26-40) runs before 'Checkout PR head' (line 42-43). Without `-R`, and with no GH_REPO env, `gh pr view` works out the repository from the git remote in the current directory. On a fresh or cleaned self-hosted workspace that directory is not a git repo, so gh exits with 'not a git repository'. That failure is inside `$(...)` passed to `echo`, so the step still succeeds and writes `head=` and `base=` as empty strings. actions/checkout then gets `ref: ''` and checks out the default ref for the dispatched branch instead of the PR head. PR_HEAD_SHA and PR_BASE_SHA reach the review step empty, so a manual review either reviews the wrong code or fails later. The step only works when a stale checkout from an earlier run happens to be left in the workspace. The pull_request path is not affected because it uses EVENT_HEAD and EVENT_BASE.

findings.title: Restore malformed-output errors in normalizeReview instead of defaulting
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, normalizeReview threw `malformed review output: ...` when the input was not an object or when summary, findings, checked or residual_risks was missing or the wrong type. Now any of those cases returns `{summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}`. Examples: null, a truncated JSON object, `{findings:"..."}`, or a reply with a misspelled key. That result has zero findings and no `blocks:true` risks, which is exactly what a clean review looks like. Anything that turns RawReview into a ReviewResult verdict would read a broken or garbage model reply as PASS. Malformed JSON that should fail the review would silently approve the PR. It also partially defaults: a valid findings array with a missing residual_risks key drops any blocking risks without saying so. normalizeReview is exported, so every caller is now forced to treat a failed reply as a valid empty review.

findings.title: Restore malformed-output errors in normalizeReview
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, normalizeReview threw 'malformed review output: ...' when raw was not an object, summary was not a string, or findings/checked/residual_risks were not arrays. Now each of those cases is replaced with a default: summary becomes String(raw?.summary ?? "") (lines 125), and findings, checked and residual_risks become [] (lines 115-128). So inputs like null, a string, or {} (for example truncated or unparsed model output) produce {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}. That is exactly what a genuine clean review looks like: no findings and no blocking residual risks. Any code that turns RawReview into a ReviewResult verdict (Verdict = pass|changes_requested|needs_human, line 22) will treat a failed or garbled review as 'pass' instead of escalating it. A non-string summary is also silently turned into a string (e.g. '[object Object]'). This is an exported public function, so every caller is forced to mix up 'the reviewer failed' with 'the reviewer found nothing'.

findings.title: Keep rejecting malformed review output instead of returning an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, normalizeReview threw 'malformed review output: ...' when the input was not an object or when summary, findings, checked or residual_risks was missing or the wrong type. Now every one of those cases is replaced with a default: summary becomes "", and findings, checked and residual_risks become []. Input like null, a JSON string, a truncated object, or an object using the wrong key name (e.g. `residualRisks` or `issues`) now comes back as {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}. That is exactly what a genuinely clean review looks like: no findings and no blocking risks. Any verdict built from RawReview (ReviewResult.verdict, schema.ts:76) will therefore treat a crashed, truncated or hallucinated reviewer response as a pass instead of an error. This is a public export, so every caller is forced to mix up 'reviewer failed' with 'no defects found'. The old checks (e.g. `checked` must be an array) were deliberately strict to prevent exactly this.

findings.title: Restore PR ref lookup for workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow still accepts `workflow_dispatch` with a required `pr_number` (lines 10-14), and the job gate at line 24 lets it run. On a manual run there is no `github.event.pull_request`, so every replacement expression falls back. Line 29 checks out `github.ref`, which is the branch the run was dispatched from (usually main), not the PR head. Line 35 fetches a hard-coded `main` instead of the PR's real base branch. Lines 45-46 set `PR_BASE_SHA` and `PR_HEAD_SHA` to empty strings. The old `Resolve PR refs` step got all three values from `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"`; this diff deletes it and puts nothing in its place. This repo reviews itself by running the checked-out `src/` (lines 3-5), so a manual run of `--pr N` runs main's copy of the tool against main's tree, not PR N's code, and the CLI gets no base/head SHAs. A PR whose base is not main is also compared against the wrong branch. The manual trigger exists to cover runs the `pull_request` webhook misses, and it now silently reviews the wrong code.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: A manual run (workflow_dispatch with pr_number) has no github.event.pull_request in its payload. Line 29 therefore resolves to github.ref, which is the branch the run was started from (usually the default branch), not the PR head. Since this repo reviews itself with its own checked-out src/ (see the comment at lines 3-5), that means the old src/cli.ts on main runs instead of the PR's code. Line 35 falls back to 'main' even when the PR targets another branch. Lines 45-46 become empty strings, so the CLI gets no base/head SHAs. The removed step looked all three values up with `gh pr view $PR_NUM` (headRefOid/baseRefOid/baseRef) for exactly this case. The 'bypasses pull_request webhook' manual trigger (line 13) now checks out the wrong commit and gives the CLI wrong or empty refs.

findings.title: Restore PR head/base resolution for workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow still accepts workflow_dispatch with a required pr_number (lines 10-14), and the job condition lets it run (line 24). A dispatch event has no github.event.pull_request payload. So `ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref` (line 29) falls back to the branch the run was dispatched from, usually main, not the PR head. fetch-depth: 0 does not fetch refs/pull/N/head, so the PR's commits may not exist locally at all. BASE_REF falls back to a hardcoded 'main' (line 35), which is wrong for PRs that target any other branch. PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA (lines 45-46) become empty strings. The removed step used `gh pr view $PR_NUM` to fill in all of these. findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git spawnSync so diffs over 1 MiB can be reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: Because the call no longer sets `maxBuffer`, spawnSync uses Node's default of 1024*1024 bytes. If `git diff baseSha HEAD` (line 100) prints more than 1 MiB, Node kills the child process and returns `status: null` with `error.code === 'ENOBUFS'`. The `res.status !== 0` check on line 12 then throws, and the message usually has an empty stderr, so the user just sees `git diff ... failed:`. Before this change the limit was 64 MiB, so medium and large PRs could be reviewed. Now `runLocal` aborts before it ever calls `review()`. The `gh` wrapper (lines 33-37) still sets 64 MiB, so this was not an intentional policy change.

findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1024*1024 bytes. runLocal calls git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) at line 100 and puts the whole patch into the bundle. If the patch is larger than 1 MiB, Node kills the child and sets res.error to ENOBUFS with status null. The `res.status !== 0` check at line 12 then throws `git diff ... failed: ` with an empty or unrelated stderr, and res.error is never shown. Before this change the limit was 64 MiB, so a medium-to-large PR that used to review fine now aborts with a confusing message. findings.title: Restore maxBuffer so git diffs larger than 1 MiB don't abort review

If stdout goes over that, Node kills the child and sets res.error=ENOBUFS, and res.status is null. findings.title: Keep review-error check conclusion as failure, not neutral
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block at lines 185-197 handles every failure in review(): model or API outages, malformed output, and inputs crafted to crash the reviewer. It used to post `conclusion: "failure"`, which blocked a required 'Needlefish' check. It now posts `"neutral"`, and GitHub branch protection treats a neutral required check as satisfied. A PR that makes the reviewer crash therefore becomes mergeable without review. The check's own text says 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR', but the new conclusion means it effectively did pass. `process.exitCode = 1` does not help here: it fails the workflow job, not the separately posted 'Needlefish' check run. Using neutral also makes a crash look the same as a real `needs_human` verdict, which also maps to neutral (line 53).

findings.title: Avoid gh pr diff, which fails on large PRs before any check is posted
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch used to come from a local `git diff baseSha HEAD`. Now it comes from `gh pr diff`, which calls GitHub's diff endpoint. That endpoint refuses diffs over its size limits (about 20k lines or 300 files) and returns an HTTP 406 'diff exceeded the maximum'. In that case ghText throws at line 143, which is outside the try/catch that starts at line 179, so no check run is posted. Large PRs that used to get reviewed now just crash the runner. Also, ghText runs without `cwd` (line 29), so `gh pr diff` picks its repo from process.cwd() rather than the `cwd` passed to runGithub. The local git calls next to it (changedFileSet, line 144) do use `cwd`, so the diff and the changed-file list can come from different places.

findings.title: Keep 'failure' conclusion when the review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block runs for any error from review(), postReview() or the success-path postCheck(). It now posts the Needlefish check-run as 'neutral'. GitHub's required status checks count 'neutral' the same as 'success', so a review that crashed, timed out or never ran now lets the PR merge. That contradicts the check's own text, 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR'. Callers of the check can no longer tell 'review failed' apart from 'no blocking result', and process.exitCode=1 only fails the Actions job, not the Needlefish check that branch protection reads.

findings.title: Pin gh pr diff to the reviewed repo instead of process cwd
findings.whyItBreaks: ghText (lines 28-34) calls spawnSync with no cwd, so `gh pr diff N` works out the repo from process.cwd()'s git remote (or GH_REPO). It ignores both the `cwd` argument and GITHUB_REPOSITORY. The old code ran `git diff` inside `cwd`, and every other gh call here uses an explicit `repos/${repo}` path. If runGithub's cwd is not the process directory, the diff call fails or pulls the diff from the wrong repo. The patch also now comes from GitHub (PR head) while changedFileSet still runs `git diff baseSha HEAD` on the local checkout. If those trees differ (e.g. a push after checkout), the reviewer gets a patch that doesn't match changedFiles or the files it reads in repoPath, and the result is posted against pr.head.sha.

findings.title: Keep 'failure' conclusion when the review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: When review(bundle) throws (LLM/tool error, timeout, gh failure inside postReview), the catch block now posts the 'Needlefish' check run with conclusion 'neutral'. GitHub branch protection treats a 'neutral' check as passing a required status check, so any PR where the review crashed is now mergeable without review. The posted summary still says 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR', which contradicts the check status. Before this change, the error reached the merge gate as 'failure' and blocked the merge. Now the gate gets a value it cannot tell apart from a legitimate non-blocking 'needs_human' result (VERDICT_CONCLUSION maps needs_human→neutral at line 53). Anyone who triggers a reviewer error, for example with a huge diff or input that makes the model fail, gets past the required gate.

findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, the reviewer was checked out from frankekn/needlefish@main into `needlefish/`, and only that copy was installed and run. The PR head sat in `target/` and was only read. Now the job checks out the PR head into the workspace root, runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` on it (L51), and runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (L59). That defeats the review gate, which is exactly what the removed comment said the old setup prevented. findings.title: Restore case/whitespace normalization and the P1 fallback for severity
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code ran `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` before checking against SEVERITIES, so "p0", "P0 " and " p1" were all accepted. The new code checks `raw.severity` exactly as given, so any lowercase or padded value fails `SEVERITIES.includes` and becomes P3. The default for missing or unrecognized severities also moved from P1 to P3. Taken together, a model saying "p0" about a security bypass now produces a P3 finding, the lowest severity. normalizeFinding is exported and is the only normalization step (normalizeReview maps it over every finding at line 132), so callers can't tell a real P3 from a bad or missing severity. Any verdict or gating logic based on severity will rank blocking findings as minor.

findings.title: Restore severity trim/uppercase and keep a conservative fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` turned "p0", " P1 " or "p2\n" into a valid severity. Now the exact-match `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity)` rejects all of them and they fall to the new default "P3". The old default was "P1". A finding the model labeled P0 is now stored as P3, which is the lowest severity and normally does not block. Missing or malformed severities also used to be treated as likely regressions (P1) and are now treated as low-risk. `normalizeFinding` is exported and runs on every finding via `normalizeReview` (schema.ts:132). The function cannot tell "model said P3" apart from "severity was garbled", so blocking findings are quietly downgraded.

findings.title: Restore severity case/whitespace normalization and fail-safe default
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code ran String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase() before checking SEVERITIES, so "p0", " P1" and "p2\n" were accepted as P0/P1/P2. The new code checks the raw value with SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity), which is exact and case-sensitive, so each of those is rejected. The fallback also changed from P1 to P3. Any lowercase, padded, or missing severity now becomes P3, the lowest level, and the caller can't tell that from a P3 the reviewer actually assigned. A model that answers "p0" for a security bypass gets stored as P3. Any verdict logic that holds merges on P0–P2 would then pass it. Before, the same input stayed at P0, and unknown values became the safer P1.

findings.title: Restore scrubbing of GitHub tokens from the codex child env
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, runCodex built a copy of process.env without GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN and passed it as `env` to spawnSync. Now spawnSync has no `env` option, so Node passes the full parent process.env to the child. `codex exec` runs an LLM agent that executes shell commands in `opts.repoPath`, and that path is a repo under review, so its content is attacker-controlled. A prompt injection in the reviewed diff or files can make the agent read the GitHub tokens (for example with `env` or `gh auth token`) and leak them through the model output or network tools. `-s read-only` only restricts filesystem writes. It does not stop the agent from reading environment variables or including secrets in its final message, which runCodex returns to the caller. The scrubbing was a deliberate least-privilege boundary, and nothing in the repo replaces it.

findings.title: Restore removal of GitHub tokens from the codex child env
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, runCodex built a copy of process.env, deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN from it, and passed that copy as `env` to spawnSync. The diff removes both the copy and the `env` option. When spawnSync gets no `env`, Node passes the full process.env to the child. The codex agent runs inside the repo under review (`cwd: opts.repoPath`) and receives the diff as its prompt (`input: prompt`), and both are controlled by whoever wrote the PR. A prompt injection can now get the agent to read the tokens from its environment and print them in its final message, which runCodex returns (lines 31-35, 45). The `-s read-only` sandbox limits file writes; it does not hide environment variables. This is a credential-exposure regression with no functional benefit.

findings.title: Restore same-repo guard before running fork PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow runs on `pull_request` (opened/synchronize/reopened) with `runs-on: self-hosted`. It checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (L23) and then runs code from that checkout: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (L28), which runs dependency lifecycle scripts, and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (L34), which is the PR's own source (the header comment says the checkout's src/ is the tool). The removed guard `github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only thing stopping fork PRs from reaching these steps. Now anyone who opens a fork PR can run any code they like on Frank's machine. Both steps use `zsh -l {0}`, so the code runs in the user's login environment, where it can read local credentials such as LLM API keys and SSH keys, change or persist on the runner, and tamper with later jobs. GitHub's lower token permissions for forks don't help here: the risk is the host, not the token.

findings.title: Restore same-repo guard before running PR code on self-hosted runner

Without it, anyone who opens a fork PR can run arbitrary code on the host. That code can read local credentials such as model API keys and gh/ssh config, and can leave persistent changes on a runner that is not ephemeral, which affects later jobs. It also gains nothing: on fork PRs GitHub gives a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN, so the `pull-requests: write`/`checks: write` review post fails anyway.

findings.title: Keep honoring an explicit 0 grace/give-up duration instead of the default
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs has two callers: NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS (default 5000, lines 3-6) and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS (default 2000, lines 7-10). Before this change, a value of 0 was accepted. 0 means 'SIGKILL right after SIGTERM' (hardKillTimer setTimeout at line 117) or 'stop waiting right after SIGKILL' (giveUpTimer at line 119), and setTimeout(fn, 0) handles that correctly. With `parsed > 0`, '0' now falls through to fallbackMs. Anyone who set either var to 0 gets 5s or 2s of extra wait on every runner timeout, with no error or log. The value they set is silently ignored and replaced by a larger one, so timeouts take longer than configured.

findings.title: Keep explicit 0ms runner durations instead of using the default
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 were accepted. They meant: send SIGKILL right after SIGTERM, and stop waiting for the child's 'close' right after SIGKILL. With `parsed > 0`, the value "0" parses to 0, fails the check, and becomes 5000 (line 5) or 2000 (line 9). Those constants feed the timers at lines 124 and 123. A user who asked for no extra wait now gets up to 7s more after timeoutMs before spawnRunnerProcess returns, and nothing warns them. 0 is a valid setTimeout delay and a valid duration, so this was never a bad input. The function is exported, so other callers also lose the ability to pass 0.

findings.title: Keep accepting 0 ms for the runner grace and give-up env overrides
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs parses only two values: NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS (line 3, default 5000) and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS (line 7, default 2000). At base, `parsed >= 0` accepted "0" as a real setting. With grace=0, setTimeout at line 117/124 sends SIGKILL right after SIGTERM. With give-up=0, line 119/123 stops waiting for 'close' right after SIGKILL. With `parsed > 0`, an explicit "0" now becomes the same fallback as a missing or garbage value, and nothing is logged. Anyone who set 0 (for example, a CI or test setup that wants a fast hard kill) now gets an extra 5 s grace plus 2 s give-up on every timed-out runner. Also, the caller can no longer tell 'operator chose 0' apart from 'invalid input'. 0 is a valid delay for setTimeout, so nothing required this change.

findings.title: Restore deep-pass residual_risks instead of hardcoding []
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass returns res.residual_risks, which can include blocks:true gaps such as an untraced sentinel or an unverifiable trigger. The loop at 103-105 now throws them away, and candidateMerged.residual_risks is hardcoded to [] at line 113. The critic gets no residuals, so pruned.residual_risks is missing them, and deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks) at line 122 can return PASS even though a deep pass said it could not reach a verdict. A 'cannot conclude' signal now looks the same as 'clean'.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop for changed files not in any hotspot
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the first MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 hotspots (line 26) get deep-reviewed. Any changed file the map pass leaves out, or that only appears in hotspot 7 or later, is never reviewed. Nothing records the gap in checked or residual_risks, so the result can PASS a PR with unreviewed files. The removed tail-coverage hotspot was the only guard against this.

findings.title: Don't let one failed deep pass abort the whole large review
findings.whyItBreaks: The try/catch is gone. If extractJson or normalizeReview throws for one hotspot (malformed model output), reviewLarge rejects, and all the map and deep work already done is lost with no partial result. Before, the failure became a blocks:true residual naming the hotspot and the review carried on.

findings.title: Keep whyItBreaks in the dedup key so separate findings don't merge
findings.whyItBreaks: The key is now file|lineStart|category plus the first 60 characters of the title. Two separate bugs at the same line and category whose titles share a 60-character prefix (common with templated titles from different hotspots) collapse into one. Only the higher-severity finding survives, so the other defect disappears before the critic sees it. Before, the first 80 characters of whyItBreaks kept them apart.

findings.title: Restore the coverage backstop for files outside the top-6 hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: The list of hotspots is sorted and cut to MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 (line 26). Changed files are covered only if the map model put them in one of those 6 hotspots. Before this change, a tail hotspot picked up every uncovered changed file, so nothing was skipped silently. Now any file the map pass dropped or ranked past 6 gets no deep review. Nothing is written to checked or residual_risks, and deriveVerdict can return PASS on a PR that was never fully reviewed.

findings.title: Pass deep-pass residual_risks to the critic instead of resetting them to []
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass returns res.residual_risks, which can include blocks=true entries meaning the reviewer could not reach a verdict. Before, these were collected in `residuals` and sent to the critic in candidateMerged. Now they are thrown away, and candidateMerged.residual_risks is always []. The critic never sees them, so pruned.residual_risks cannot carry them, and deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks) at line 122 can return PASS when a deep reviewer said it could not decide. A 'blocked' result now looks the same as 'clean'.

findings.title: Restore per-hotspot try/catch so one failing deep pass doesn't abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: Before, if extractJson or normalizeReview failed for one hotspot (malformed model output, codex error), the code recorded 'DEEP PASS FAILED' and added a blocking residual risk, and the other hotspots still ran. Now that exception escapes reviewLarge. One bad model response throws away every finding already collected from the other hotspots and fails the whole large-PR review. Before, the result was a reported, blocked review.

findings.title: Keep whyItBreaks in the dedup key so distinct findings aren't merged
findings.whyItBreaks: The dedup key is now file|lineStart|category|first 60 chars of the title. Two different defects from different hotspots at the same anchor line and category, with similar generic titles (for example 'Handle error in ...'), now share a key. The lower-severity one is dropped silently, so a real finding never reaches the critic or the final output. Before, the key also included the first 80 chars of whyItBreaks, which kept distinct defects apart.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual_risks to the critic instead of dropping them
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass returns its own residual_risks (`res.residual_risks`), which can include blocks=true entries. Before this change they were collected into `residuals` and passed to the critic in `candidateMerged.residual_risks`. Now the loop ignores `res.residual_risks` and `candidateMerged` hard-codes `residual_risks: []`. The critic never sees a deep pass's blocking gap, so `deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks)` (line 122) gets no blocking risk and can return PASS. A review that should block is reported as clean.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so files outside the hotspots still get reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: `hotspots` is the map output after `.slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (6). A changed file can miss deep review in two ways: the map pass never assigned it to a hotspot, or it only belongs to hotspots ranked 7th or lower. The removed block added those files to a tail-coverage hotspot. Without it, those files are never deep-reviewed. Nothing goes into checked or residual_risks to say so, so a large PR can PASS with changed files nobody looked at.

findings.title: Keep whyItBreaks in the dedup key so distinct findings aren't merged
findings.whyItBreaks: The key used to include the first 80 characters of whyItBreaks, normalized. Now it is only file|lineStart|category plus the first 60 characters of the title. Two deep passes, often from overlapping hotspots, can report different defects at the same line and category with generic titles such as "Handle error from parse". These now share a key, and only the higher-severity one is kept, so a real finding is silently lost before the critic sees it.

findings.title: Restore focus/deep propagation in reviewLarge map and deep prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: `bundle.focus` and `bundle.deep` are still bundle fields: the input bundle has them, and the small-PR path (`review.ts:52-55`) passes the whole bundle into review.md. In the large-PR path, which runs when the patch is over 30000 chars or touches more than 10 files (`isLarge`, line 30-31), the diff drops `focus` and `deep` from `mapBundle` (lines 83-89) and removes the `{{FOCUS}}` substitution from the deep prompt chain. So whether the user's focus is honoured now depends on PR size: large PRs ignore it with no warning, and the map pass loses the deep flag it used to get. Base explicitly replaced `{{FOCUS}}` in deep.md. If that placeholder is still in the template, the deep reviewer now sees a literal `{{FOCUS}}` instead of the focus or "(none)".

findings.title: Restore {{FOCUS}} substitution in the per-hotspot deep prompt
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code filled the `{{FOCUS}}` placeholder in deep.md with `bundle.focus ?? "(none)"`. The head deletes that step and adds nothing to replace it. On large PRs (isLarge: patch > 30000 chars or > 10 files), the deep pass never learns the user's focus. If deep.md still contains `{{FOCUS}}`, the model now sees the raw text `{{FOCUS}}` instead of a value. Small PRs still pass focus, because reviewSmall serializes the whole bundle at lines 52-55. So focus is silently ignored only when the PR is large.

findings.title: Keep focus/deep in the map-pass bundle
findings.whyItBreaks: mapBundle no longer includes `focus` or `deep`. The map pass picks the hotspots (sortByRisk, then slice to MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 at line 96), so it now chooses them without the user's focus or deep request. The area the user asked about can rank below the cut. It is then only picked up by the low-risk tail-coverage backstop, and with the deep-prompt focus also removed, nothing points the reviewer at it. Small PRs still send both fields (whole bundle at line 54), so behavior differs by PR size.

findings.title: Restore focus substitution in deep-pass prompt for large PRs
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code replaced `{{FOCUS}}` in deep.md with `bundle.focus ?? "(none)"`. That line is now gone. In reviewLarge, the deep pass is the only step that reviews each hotspot, so a caller's focus never reaches it. If deep.md still contains `{{FOCUS}}`, which the base replacement strongly suggests, the prompt also carries a raw, unfilled placeholder. reviewSmall (lines 51-55) still serializes the whole bundle, including focus and deep. So the same request behaves differently depending only on PR size: the focus is honored for small PRs and silently ignored for large ones (more than 10 files or more than 30000 patch characters).

findings.title: Round once before splitting minutes/seconds to avoid '1m 60s'
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes is floored from raw ms, but seconds is rounded separately from the leftover ms. Any leftover of 59500–59999 ms rounds up to 60. Examples: ms=119500 gives minutes=1 and seconds=round(59.5)=60, so the output is '1m 60s' (old code: '2m 0s'). ms=59500 gives '60s' (old code: '1m 0s'). The markdown report shows these wrong durations for each stage (line 75) and for the total (line 80).

findings.title: Round to total seconds before splitting minutes to avoid "60s"
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code works out minutes from the raw ms first and only then rounds the leftover seconds. When the leftover is between 59500 and 59999 ms, the seconds round up to 60 without adding a minute. For example, 119500 ms gives minutes=1 and seconds=round(59.5)=60, so it shows "1m 60s" (the old code showed "2m 0s"). 59500 ms shows "60s" (the old code showed "1m 0s"). This is a regression in the per-call and total durations that renderMarkdown prints in the review report's stats line (lines 75 and 80).

findings.title: Round to whole seconds before splitting into minutes and seconds
findings.whyItBreaks: The minutes come from flooring the raw milliseconds, but the seconds are rounded separately from the remainder. When the remainder is 59500–59999 ms, Math.round gives 60. So ms=119500 renders as "1m 60s" (the old code gave "2m 0s"), and ms=59500 renders as "60s" (the old code gave "1m 0s"). These strings show up in the markdown review output, in each stage's duration and in the total.

findings.title: Restore rejection of zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The function's name and its error text (`requires a positive integer`) promise a value >= 1. With `parsed < 0`, the input "0" returns 0. Because Number("") and Number("  ") are also 0, an empty or whitespace-only flag/env value now parses as 0 without an error instead of being rejected. This is an exported public function, so any caller that relies on the promise (timeouts, counts, concurrency, retry limits, divisors) gets 0. That can mean an instant timeout, zero workers or a division by zero, and the error message no longer describes what is actually checked.

findings.title: Restore rejection of zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so `"0"` now returns 0. Because Number('') and Number('  ') both evaluate to 0, an empty or whitespace-only input also returns 0 instead of throwing. A caller that trusts the promise for things like a timeout, retry count or concurrency limit would get a zero timeout, zero attempts or a divide-by-zero, and a blank CLI or env value would quietly become 0 instead of failing validation.

findings.whyItBreaks: The check changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so 0 is now returned as a valid value. RunnerOptions.timeoutMs is a typical value for this parser, and a 0 there leads to an instant timeout or a zero-sized budget. Callers rely on the name and get a value it says can't happen.
